content: Vitamers are the various chemical compounds that exhibit the biological activity of a specific vitamin. Unlike the common perception that a vitamin is a single compound, most vitamins are actually represented by multiple substances, all of which contribute to the same biological function. The definition of a vitamin is based on its biological activity rather than its chemical structure. The activity of different vitamers within the same vitamin group is often due to the body's limited ability to convert one vitamer into another or to transform multiple vitamers into the same enzymatic cofactor(s). This limitation exists despite the fact that the body cannot synthesize an adequate amount of the vitamin from basic dietary components without the presence of at least one vitamer as a precursor. This variation arises from differences in how the body absorbs and metabolizes the various vitamers. Similarly, the toxicity of vitamers can differ depending on their molecular structure. For instance, the different forms of vitamin E exhibit varying levels of toxicity. In some cases, a group of related vitamers is categorized under a generic descriptor, such as vitamin A. For example, vitamin A includes compounds like retinal, retinol, and several carotenoids. Another example is vitamin B-12, which encompasses cyanocobalamin, hydroxocobalamin, methylcobalamin, and 5-deoxyadenosylcobalamin (also known as adenosylcobalamin or AdoB-12). All of these compounds share B-12 activity. Similarly, both niacinamide and nicotinic acid (niacin) exhibit vitamin B-3 activity. Some vitamins, such as biotin and folate, have not been assigned specific alphabetic generic descriptors by naming conventions. These are still considered B vitamins but lack a specific B number. Even in these cases, the vitamins consist of multiple active vitamers that are present in foods and play distinct roles in cellular functions.
